title: NgModule versus standalone
summary: Recognise the older NgModule style and convert it to a standalone component.

quiz.q: In a standalone component, where do you list the other components, directives and pipes its template uses?
quiz.explain: A standalone component carries its own dependencies in `imports`, so you can read one file and see everything it needs.

quiz.q: Which function starts a standalone app?
quiz.explain: `bootstrapApplication` takes the root component and the app config. The second option is the old module way.

quiz.q: You open an older project and see `@NgModule({ declarations: [AppComponent] })`. What does `declarations` do?
options: Registers components that belong to that module
quiz.explain: In the module style, a component belonged to exactly one module through `declarations`. Standalone components removed that extra step.

quiz.q: Complete the setting a standalone component uses to list the modules, components and pipes its template needs.
quiz.explain: A standalone component lists its own dependencies in `imports`.

exercise.task:
Convert `main.ts` from the NgModule style to standalone.

- Delete the `@NgModule` class `AppModule`.
- Remove the `standalone: false` setting from `AppComponent`.
- Give `AppComponent` `imports: [FormsModule]`.
- Bootstrap with `bootstrapApplication(AppComponent)` imported from `@angular/platform-browser`.
hints: A standalone component needs no module. Remove the module class and its bootstrap call.
What the module imported (`FormsModule`) moves into the component's own `imports` list.

checks.name: There is no @NgModule
checks.hint: Delete the AppModule class and its @NgModule decorator.

checks.name: AppComponent no longer says standalone: false
checks.hint: Remove standalone: false from the @Component settings.

checks.name: The old bootstrapModule call is gone
